newsitem.title: USA: SHOPPING BAGS: old standards become fashion statement.
newsitem.headline: SHOPPING BAGS: old standards become fashion statement.

text.p: It used to be, you are what you eat. Today, you are what you tote -- your shopping bag.

Not too long ago, shopping bags were nothing more than brown kraft paper sachels with rope handles. Most shoppers took their purchases home in boxes or in wrapped packages. Not until the 1950s did retailers recognise shopping bags as prime marketing tools.

Today, shopping bags are some stores' only advertising and a status symbol for the carrier. You may have your lunch in a Tiffany's bag, or dirty shirts in a Bloomingdale's bag but the cachet of the stores is what people notice.

While styles and stores come and go, the future of shopping bags is secure. In fact, says a manufacturer of shopping bags, these products are often on the cutting edge of style, defining today what styles may be tomorrow. Bag designers take their work as seriously as fashion designers.
The designer shopping bag craze really started at Bloomingdale's in the mid-1960s. Major retailers had image-defining shopping bags, such as Macy's burgundy bags with the Macy's star.

Yet, at Bloomingdale's, then-store-President Marvin Traub realised that people buy more if they have something roomy to put it in. And, if the shopping bag was attractive and trendy, that would reflect on the store.

"Marvin Traub recognised the virtue of shopping bags and they gave away 8 to 9 million shopping bags a year at the 59th Street (flagship) store," said manufacturer and shopping bag collector Ron Basso.
"They projected the image of the store on the shopping bag, hardly using the Bloomingdale's name at all," he said.
This started an avalanche of copy-cats, with stores of all stripes changing shopping bag styles as they changed merchandise.
However, with the retail downturn that began in the late 1980s, stores needed something to get customers excited. And, Basso believes, it was the bag.

The bags of 1997 and beyond will take the shape of traditional shopping bags, the handled square or rectangular bag with gussets on the sides and bottom, but will act as a design bridge to the 21st century.
Only low-end shopping bags will use brown paper, and those will be seen less and less, he said. Polycoatings or clay coatings will be used to give the bags texture. And, there will be plastic.
Plastic is "strong and lends itself to great colour projection in the material as well as printing effects," he said.
At the Gap, for example, its new holiday sales bag is a sturdy translucent plastic bag. Coloured tissue paper wraps the merchandise.

The clear plastic bags have dual purposes, Basso said. "They appeal to virtually every creative director in retailing," meaning that they are on the cutting edge of fashion. Also, "Security loves the bags.
"Rarely do these two areas come together."

Colours print well on plastic, leading to strong, computer driven graphics. Shoppers will be seeing more and more colour printed plastic bags -- traditional bag shapes with unusual printed designs. Handles will most likely be made of rigid plastic, Basso said.

Basso is general manager of Continental Extrusion, a manufacturer of upscale shopping bags. The company is owned by The Jim Pattison Group, of Vancouver, British Columbia. He said the company's Cedar Grove, N.J., plant produces 20 million to 25 million bags a year.
Nationwide, about 100 million shopping bags are used a year, with 40 million to 50 million designated for holiday shoppers.

Even as a shopping bag may be worth millions in advertising, shoppers don't realise that they, in effect, pay for the bag every time they make a purchase. Basso said that a fancy shopping bag costs a retailer 20 cents to 30 cents each. That cost, as always, is passed on to the shopper.
